title: Branded Types
summary: Distinguish values that share a basic type but represent different meanings.
nestedConcepts: Add a brand to a primitive type

subtopics.title: Add a brand to a primitive type
subtopics.explanation: A branded type intersects a basic type with a unique marker, making two otherwise identical values distinct to the type checker. For example, `UserId` and `OrderId` can both be strings but cannot be passed interchangeably. The marker exists for checking, not as a runtime feature.

subtopics.title: Use brands for validated values
subtopics.explanation: Brands are useful when a value has passed a meaningful check or represents a distinct unit. A validated email can have a different type from arbitrary input text. Keep the brand tied to a real validation rule; otherwise it only makes code harder to construct.

subtopics.title: Create brands through validation
subtopics.explanation: Create a branded value through a function that checks its input and returns the branded type only when the check passes. For example, parse an ID string before returning `UserId`. This keeps the type promise in one place instead of allowing unchecked casts throughout the app.

subtopics.title: Validate external data first
subtopics.explanation: Values from a request, storage, or user input should begin as `unknown`, because TypeScript cannot verify data arriving at runtime. Check the required shape and constraints before creating a brand. A compile-time type annotation cannot make untrusted data valid.

subtopics.title: Remember brands are compile-time only
subtopics.explanation: A brand is erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript; it does not add a runtime marker or change the underlying value. Use a runtime check when behavior depends on the distinction. Brands help prevent accidental mixing during development, but they are not security boundaries.

foundations.overview: A branded type adds a compile-time marker to a primitive or object type. For example, UserId and OrderId may both be strings, but should not be interchanged. The brand does not validate data at runtime, so input still needs checking.
foundations.mentalModel: Two keys may have the same shape but open different doors.
foundations.whyItMatters: It prevents accidental mixing of values that look identical to JavaScript.

keyTakeaways: A brand adds a unique marker property to a type.
Brands can distinguish IDs, validated email, or units.
Construct branded values through a validation function.
External data begins as unknown and must be checked.

codeLab.title: Keep User IDs and Order IDs Separate
codeLab.instructions: Add brands so a function requiring a UserId cannot accidentally receive an OrderId.
codeLab.expectedOutput: The type checker accepts safe values and reports mismatches at compile time.
hints: Keep external values typed as unknown until you check them.
Use a type feature that preserves the exact information you need.
